t: Evaluate the Bracket Pairs of a String: Hash-Map Substitution
o: The string s interleaves literal lowercase text with bracketed keys, and knowledge maps each key to a value; every bracket pair must be replaced by its key's value, or by the literal ? when the key is unknown, and the resulting string returned. Example 1: (name)is(age)yearsold with name -> bob and age -> two becomes bobistwoyearsold. Example 2 shows unknown keys collapsing to ?, and Example 3 confirms that text outside brackets is untouched. Sizes are moderate (|s| up to 10^5, up to 10^5 known keys of length at most 10), so loading knowledge into a hash map once and scanning s once gives linear total time; brackets never nest, which means no stack is needed — a simple index scan or even regex substitution suffices.
k: Load knowledge into a hash map up front so each bracket resolves in time proportional to its key length.
Brackets are guaranteed non-nested and well-formed, so left-to-right scanning with indexOf for the closing parenthesis is sufficient — no stack required.
Unknown keys must render as exactly ?, while known keys substitute their full value.
Assemble output in a resizable buffer (StringBuilder / list join), since repeated string concatenation degrades to quadratic.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Index Scanning
a.i: Walk i across s appending ordinary characters; upon hitting an opening parenthesis, locate the matching close with indexOf, look up the inner slice in the map, append either the stored value or ?, and jump past the closing bracket. One pass, no auxiliary structures beyond the map and output buffer.
s: Build map kv from knowledge pairs.
Scan i from 0: if s[i] is not an opening bracket, append it and advance.
Otherwise find the next closing bracket j, extract the key s[i+1..j), and append kv.get(key) or ?.
Continue from j + 1 until the string ends; join and return the buffer.
a.t: O(|s| + total knowledge size) — building the map touches every key once and the scan visits each character once.
a.sp: O(total knowledge size + |s|) — the map plus the output buffer.

a.i: A pattern capturing anything between parentheses matches exactly the well-formed, non-nested pairs the constraints promise. Substituting every match through a callback that consults the map (defaulting to ?) collapses the whole task into one expression. Constant-factor overhead from the regex engine is irrelevant at these sizes, and the code shrinks dramatically.
s: Compile a pattern like [(]([a-z]+)[)] capturing the key inside the brackets.
Look up each captured key in the map during substitution, emitting ? on miss.
Apply the substitution globally over s and return the result.
a.t: O(|s| + total knowledge size) — the automaton scans each character a constant number of times; map construction is unchanged.
a.sp: O(total knowledge size + |s|) — dictionary plus match state and output.

w: Use the manual scan as your primary answer — it makes the linear-time claim obvious and ports to any language; mention the regex version as a concise alternative when allowed library magic. Pitfalls: defaulting missing keys to something other than exactly ?, concatenating onto an immutable string inside the loop (quadratic blowup on 10^5 characters), assuming nested brackets after forgetting the constraint guarantees, and mishandling adjacent pairs like (a)(b). Edge cases: a string with no brackets, keys repeated many times in s (each resolved independently), and values containing characters like parentheses themselves — worth asking about in an interview since it would break naive regex splitting. Follow-up: support nested brackets (requires a stack-based evaluator) or streaming evaluation over a character stream.
